question: How well can independently initialized finite-depth random-feature subnetworks approximate functions in neural-network Gaussian-process RKHSs, and how does that function class compare with two-layer Barron space?

key_findings.claim: Functions in a finite-width expected-kernel RKHS can be approximated at a Monte Carlo rate by an ensemble of independent multilayer random-feature subnetworks.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 states that for bounded activation sigma, any f in the RKHS of the finite expected depth-L kernel admits T independent random subnetworks with trained final linear coefficients and L2 error at most the activation bound times the RKHS norm divided by square root T. The construction is block-parallel: subnetworks are independent below the last linear combination.

key_findings.claim: Finite hidden-layer widths contribute inverse-width kernel variance and approximation error terms.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 bounds empirical-kernel variance by a sum of terms proportional to 1/n_i, amplified through depth-dependent constants. Theorem 3 compares finite expected and infinite NNGP kernels under bounded derivatives through fourth order. Theorem 4 combines these bounds with output Monte Carlo error, yielding an O(1/square-root-minimum-width) approximation rate when depth and smoothness constants are treated as controlled.

anchors.section: 4 Main results, Theorem 4 finite-width NNGP-RKHS approximation

key_findings.claim: The headline multilayer result does not directly cover ordinary ReLU networks, although the paper gives a clipped-ReLU bridge.
key_findings.evidence: The finite-versus-infinite kernel analysis assumes a bounded activation with bounded derivatives up to order four, excluding ReLU. The authors note that a clipped ReLU can approximate or represent the relevant construction with ReLU units, but this changes the activation and does not give the same clean constants for standard dense ReLU training.

anchors.section: 4 Main results: smoothness assumptions for the multilayer result

key_findings.claim: For slowly decaying spherical kernel spectra, the NNGP RKHS contains functions with unbounded Barron norm despite bounded RKHS norm.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5 gives an eigenvalue-growth condition under which the NNGP-RKHS unit ball is unbounded in Barron norm; ReLU- and step-induced kernels satisfy the stated slow-decay regime. Theorem 6 gives a sufficient fast-decay condition for bounded inclusion, and Theorems 7 and 8 calculate rapid decay for smoother Gaussian and sinusoidal activations.

anchors.section: 4.1 A relationship with the Barron space, Theorems 5 and 6
4.1 A relationship with the Barron space, Theorems 7 and 8

key_findings.claim: Spectral and target-function experiments illustrate activation-dependent differences but do not validate a complete theory of trained-network learnability.
key_findings.evidence: On sphere samples with M=N=20,000, empirical kernel eigenvalue slopes for ReLU are about 2.7-2.9 rather than the expected 1.5, which the authors attribute to inaccurate finite spectral estimation. Random-feature regression on spherical harmonics follows activation spectra more closely, whereas all-weight optimization changes the pattern and can erase initialization effects.

key_findings.claim: Finite trained networks display behavior that conflicts with a naive NNGP or NTK hardness prediction.
key_findings.evidence: Two-layer width-256 and width-1024 networks trained by Adam over five runs learn Gaussian-activation spherical harmonics nontrivially through degrees 1-21, while cosine fails around degree 14 and ReLU around degree 10. This ordering is opposite a simple inference from the corresponding infinite-kernel spectra, and the paper explicitly concludes that none of the compared theories fully explains optimization.

key_findings.claim: The approximation theorems are existence results for a special architecture, not sample-complexity, generalization, or end-to-end training guarantees.
key_findings.evidence: The output coefficients are chosen by an RKHS representation or fitted linear regression, and the proof does not show that finite labeled data recover them stably. Constants can grow with depth, the subnetworks are independent blocks rather than a generic dense network, and no conditioning or optimization guarantee is supplied for the supervised last-layer solve.

anchors.section: 4 Main results, Theorem 1 architecture and statement

method.core_idea: Interpret depth-L randomly initialized neural subnetworks as finite Monte Carlo features for an NNGP kernel, quantify their finite-width approximation error, and compare the resulting RKHS with classical Barron function space through spherical spectra.
method.mechanism: Sample independent multilayer feature blocks, train only their final linear combination, and use RKHS integral representations plus variance bounds to obtain T- and width-dependent approximation rates. On spheres, expand zonal kernels in spherical harmonics and relate eigenvalue decay to Barron norms, then compare the predictions with empirical kernel regression and all-weight neural-network training.
assumptions: The target belongs to the finite or infinite NNGP RKHS under the chosen activation and data measure.
Activations are bounded, and the finite-to-infinite multilayer analysis additionally has bounded derivatives through fourth order.
Depth-dependent constants remain moderate when an asymptotic width rate is interpreted practically.
Independent random-feature blocks and an optimized last layer are an acceptable approximation architecture.
The sphere-specific spectral conditions are informative for broader neural-network approximation behavior.

techniques.role: Builds a target approximation by linearly combining independent frozen random subnetworks.
Defines the target function class induced by infinite-width network covariance kernels.
Bounds empirical and expected random-network kernels through layerwise variance propagation.
Relates activation smoothness and kernel eigenvalue decay to representational function classes.
Constructs conditions under which NNGP-RKHS functions require arbitrarily large Barron norm.
Tests kernel and trained-network predictions on targets of increasing spherical frequency.

evaluations.setting: Empirical one-hidden-layer NNGP/random-feature kernels on S^2 (n=3) with M=N=20,000
evaluations.metric: Log-log decay slope of estimated eigenvalues
evaluations.result: Activation-dependent decay is visible, but estimated ReLU slopes around 2.7-2.9 disagree strongly with the predicted 1.5 asymptote.
evaluations.baseline: Analytic asymptotic eigenvalue predictions for ReLU, Gaussian, and sinusoidal activations

evaluations.setting: Random-feature regression on spherical-harmonic targets of increasing degree
evaluations.metric: Learned target error versus harmonic degree
evaluations.result: Frozen-feature performance broadly follows which harmonic eigenvalues the activation kernel supports.
evaluations.baseline: Different activations and the corresponding empirical spectrum

evaluations.setting: Two-layer width-256 and width-1024 networks trained end-to-end with Adam across five runs
evaluations.result: Gaussian networks retain nontrivial learning through degree 21, cosine fails around 14, and ReLU around 10, contradicting a simple infinite-kernel difficulty ordering.
evaluations.baseline: Frozen random features and NTK/NNGP spectral expectations

evaluations.setting: Appendix experiments varying sphere dimension (n=3 or 6), random-feature count, hidden width, and RFM versus standard initialization
evaluations.metric: Qualitative stability of spectral and learning trends
evaluations.result: Several trends persist, but finite-sample spectral accuracy and optimizer dependence remain substantial.

limitations: The principal guarantee is approximation existence, not finite-sample generalization or optimization success.
The constructive network is an ensemble of independent feature blocks rather than a conventional fully connected dense network.
Smoothness assumptions exclude standard ReLU from the clean multilayer finite-width theorem.
Depth-dependent constants may erase the apparent width rate in realistic regimes.
The Barron comparison is specialized to spherical domains and eigenvalue asymptotics.
Experiments use synthetic harmonics and display mismatches between finite networks and every compared kernel theory.
No conditioning or labeled-sample bound is given for estimating last-layer coefficients.
failure_modes: A target has small NNGP-RKHS norm but requires unstable, very large output coefficients on sampled features.
Finite widths are too small for asymptotic kernel concentration, especially at depth.
Kernel eigenvalues near numerical precision produce badly biased empirical decay slopes.
Full-network training leaves the lazy or random-feature regime and reverses kernel-based predictions.
Activation clipping used to bridge ReLU changes approximation constants or target behavior.
Sphere-specific function-class separation fails to transfer to nonuniform, structured real data.
reusable_insights: Separate representation existence, coefficient recovery, generalization, and optimization when interpreting approximation theory.
Report depth-dependent constants alongside asymptotic width exponents.
Use high-frequency eigenfunctions to stress-test the distinction between frozen features and feature learning.
Check numerical spectral estimates against known analytic asymptotics before inferring function-class behavior.
Treat NNGP, NTK, and Barron analyses as complementary regime descriptions rather than universal training theories.
open_questions: Can comparable finite-width bounds cover ordinary dense ReLU networks without clipping?
What labeled-sample and conditioning guarantees recover the promised last-layer approximation?
How do the constants scale sharply with depth and heterogeneous hidden-layer widths?
Which theory predicts the observed advantage of fully trained Gaussian networks on high-degree harmonics?
Does the NNGP-versus-Barron separation imply practical savings on natural data distributions?
Can feature-learning dynamics be quantified as a controlled departure from the random-feature ensemble?

competitive_landscape.title: Toward Deeper Understanding of Neural Networks: The Power of Initialization and a Dual View on Expressivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Daniely and colleagues connect random initialization, compositional kernels, and network expressivity. The reviewed work gives explicit finite multilayer NNGP-RKHS approximation and width-error bounds plus a Barron-space comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Neural Networks as Gaussian Processes
competitive_landscape.difference: Lee and colleagues establish the deep infinite-width Gaussian-process correspondence and evaluate GP inference. The reviewed paper asks how finite random feature blocks approximate functions in the induced RKHS and quantifies deviation from the infinite kernel.

competitive_landscape.title: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality with Convex Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Bach develops convex and random-feature analyses for two-layer networks over a Barron-like variation norm. The reviewed work demonstrates that some slowly decaying NNGP RKHSs contain functions whose Barron norm is arbitrarily large, under sphere-specific conditions.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: NTK theory describes lazy all-weight training through a fixed limiting kernel. The reviewed work centers frozen multilayer random features and empirically shows that finite all-weight optimization can behave unlike both NNGP and NTK spectral predictions.

novelty_assessment: The paper contributes a rigorous bridge from finite independent multilayer random features to NNGP-RKHS approximation, together with a notable sphere-based separation from Barron space. These extend mature random-feature and infinite-width-kernel traditions rather than replacing them. Practical claims should remain narrow: the theorems do not explain generic dense-network optimization, and the paper's own harmonic experiments make that gap unusually visible.
reviewer_notes: Read all 24 extracted pages, including Theorems 1-8, proof outlines and assumptions, ReLU/clipped-ReLU discussion, Barron comparison, main and appendix experiments, and conclusions. Primary arXiv sources were checked for deep random features, NNGP, Barron/convex networks, and NTK. The review preserves the distinction between the block-ensemble existence construction and ordinary end-to-end neural-network learning.
